design.about: Holds design references for the Workbench user interface: HTML mockups and written instructions for turning the current UI into the redesigned layout. It isn't application code. Developers use it as a spec when they change the renderer's layout, hierarchy and styling.

files.bot-chat-mockup.html: HTML mockup of the chat view for bots.
files.REDESIGN.md: Instructions for reworking the UI's layout, hierarchy and styling to match the redesign mockup.

docs.about: Project documentation outside the code: a note on the tools that chats inside the Workbench still lack, in the order to build them, and the app screenshot shown in the README.

files.agent-tools.md: Lists the tools agents still lack, in the order to build them.
files.screenshot.png: Screenshot of the app, shown in the README.

preview.about: Groups preview material for the app. Its only content is a subagents folder, with no files of its own at this level, so nothing here shows what the rest of the project uses it for.

resources.about: Holds the app's icon artwork, which the packaging step and the main process use. The app icon comes in macOS, Windows and PNG/SVG formats, and template images serve as the menu bar (tray) icon that stays visible while the app runs without a window. A mac subfolder holds further macOS-specific resources.

files.icon.icns: macOS app icon used when building the app bundle.
files.icon.ico: Windows app icon used for the installer and executable.
files.icon.png: PNG app icon, for window icons and Linux builds.
files.icon.svg: Vector source artwork for the app icon.
files.trayTemplate.png: Menu bar tray icon template image at standard resolution.
files.trayTemplate.svg: Vector source artwork for the menu bar tray icon.
files.trayTemplate@2x.png: Retina (2x) version of the menu bar tray icon template.

scripts.about: Development helper scripts. On macOS it registers the dev Electron build as a proper "Datapad Workbench" app bundle under its bundle ID, so the app has the right name and identity while developing. It replaces shells left under the app's old name and never overwrites a release build installed from GitHub Releases.

files.register-mac-app.mjs: Registers the dev Electron shell as a macOS app; skips real release installs.

src.about: The whole application source, split along Electron's process boundaries. The main process owns persistence, agents and IPC, the preload bridges it to the UI, the renderer draws the React interface, and shared holds the types and helpers both sides use.

src/main.about: The Electron main process: it stores projects, chats, bots and settings on disk, runs chat turns through the Grok and Claude Code agents over ACP, and answers the renderer over IPC. It also covers permissions, checkpoints, git worktrees, the BrowserPane and its MCP tools, code indexing, the knowledge vault, notifications, the tray menu, themes, voice and auto-updates. Everything the UI shows or does goes through this layer.

themes.about: The built-in appearance themes that ship with the app, one JSON file each. Users pick between them and can also import and export custom themes.

list.name: Projects
list.about: A project is a folder on disk that the user adds to the sidebar so they can run chats against it. Adding one through the new project modal saves it in the persistent store with a color and an icon. The icon is found by looking for the project's app icon, favicon or logo. The sidebar lists each project with its worktrees and chats, and a drag grip lets the user reorder them. Picking a project scopes new chats, the git pane, the code index and the knowledge vault to that folder.

list.name: Chat Sessions over ACP
list.about: Every chat runs as an agent session over the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), on either `grok agent stdio` or the Claude Code ACP adapter. When the user sends a message, the renderer calls the IPC bridge and the main process starts or resumes the session for that chat. The turn's prompt goes to the agent process, and the main process streams events back and waits for the turn to end. Several chats can run at the same time, each in its own session, and each can be stopped or waited on separately.

list.name: Live Turn Streaming
list.about: While an agent works, its output reaches the UI as a stream of live events. The main process forwards each event from the ACP session to the renderer. The workspace context collects these events per chat. Stream status is worked out from them separately from the reply text, so the UI knows whether a chat is running, finished or failed. The chat pane draws the live reply, and the agent reply component folds earlier tool steps and splits the reply at its step breaks.

list.name: Agent CLI Detection
list.about: Before a chat can run, the Workbench has to find the agent CLIs installed on the machine. It locates the Grok CLI and checks its version, channel, models and sign-in status. It also locates the Claude Code CLI and its ACP adapter and checks whether the user is signed in. Claude Code plan usage limits are fetched and cached, and the status bar shows them with a countdown to the next reset. The settings modal shows sign-in state for each agent.

list.name: Session Import
list.about: Chats started outside the Workbench show up in the sidebar for their project. The main process lists Grok sessions under ~/.grok/sessions and Claude Code JSONL transcripts that belong to the project folder. Large JSONL files are read row by row in chunks, so a long transcript doesn't have to be loaded at once. The imported sessions appear as chats that can be read and continued. Sessions the user hides are recorded in the store.

list.name: Persistence Store
list.about: The main process keeps all state on disk under Electron's userData/workbench folder: projects, handoffs, MCP servers, the theme, hidden sessions and bots. Writes go through keyed locks and atomic file replacement, so concurrent updates can't interleave and a crash can't leave a half-written file. Reads are safe against corruption and recover from a bad JSON file. The window's size and position are saved separately.

list.name: IPC Bridge
list.about: The React UI never touches Electron directly. The preload script builds one API object, exposes it on `window`, and declares its type for the renderer. Each call on that object becomes an IPC message that a handler registered in the main process answers. The main process also pushes events back to the renderer, such as stream updates and notices, and the UI contexts subscribe to them.

list.name: Permission Modes
list.about: Each chat session has a permission mode that sets what the agent may do without asking. When the agent requests a tool permission, the main process checks it against the session's mode. It also checks whether another chat is editing the same files and reports that as an edit clash. The chat pane shows a clash bar so the user can see the conflict, and permission activity is recorded for the activity feed.

list.name: Checkpoints
list.about: Before an agent's tool changes a file, the main process takes a snapshot of that file. At the end of each turn, the snapshots are saved as a checkpoint for that turn. This keeps a record of what the files looked like before the turn, so its changes can be reviewed or undone.

list.name: Git Worktrees
list.about: A chat can work in its own git worktree, so concurrent chats don't edit the same checkout. When a chat starts, the main process decides whether it needs isolation and, if so, creates a worktree for it. All of the app's git writes are serialized per repository by a shared lock. When a worktree is no longer used, processes still running from it are found and killed. The sidebar lists worktrees under their project.

list.name: Git Pane
list.about: The git pane is a right-side pane showing the repository state for the current project or worktree. The main process collects a git snapshot: changed and uncommitted files, branches and commits. The pane draws the changed files and a branch graph with a colored lane for each branch, plus a status line. It refreshes as chats change files.

list.name: BrowserPane
list.about: The BrowserPane is a web view built into the Workbench, so pages open inside the app instead of an external browser. The main process manages its web contents, cleans up URLs, keeps the page's console log and tracks its state. Actions such as navigate, back, forward, reload, screenshot, snapshot, click and type run one at a time through a serialized driver. The renderer component shows the page next to the chat.

list.name: Browser MCP Server
list.about: Agents control the BrowserPane through a stdio MCP server that the Workbench adds to each chat session. The agent calls a tool such as navigate or screenshot. The MCP script forwards the call to a local HTTP server in the main process, which runs it through the browser driver and returns the result. The same server also carries the Workbench's chat tools. The main process builds the MCP config and agent hooks that wire this server into each session.

list.name: Page Annotation
list.about: The user can point at parts of a page in the BrowserPane and attach notes to them. Starting annotation injects picker scripts into the page, which let the user select an element and can be cancelled or cleaned up. Each pick becomes a note in a queue in the pane. The user then sends the queued notes to the chat as context for the agent.

list.name: Chat-to-Chat Tools
list.about: Agents can talk to other chats and to bots through tools on the Workbench MCP server. An agent can send a message to another chat, ask a bot a question, or post a message to a bot's chat. The main process routes the message to the target session and starts a turn there. It returns the reply where needed and raises a notice. This lets one chat hand work to another, or coordinate several chats, as the subagents panel shows.

list.name: Bots
list.about: A bot is a persistent agent with its own folder, avatar, session rules and Agent Skills. Creating a bot sets up its folder and saves it. A bot's page has a Chat tab and a Settings tab, and skills can be added from skills.sh or well-known sites. When a bot posts a message, a toast appears in the bottom-right corner (at most three stacked), and read tracking marks bot chats as seen. Bots and their next runs also appear in the menu bar tray.

list.name: Scheduled Runs
list.about: A bot can run a prompt on a schedule written as a five-field cron expression. The cron parser finds the next matching local time, and when that time comes, the prompt is sent to the schedule's chat as a new turn. Each schedule's chat is listed indented under its bot in the sidebar, with the time until its next run. Above the messages, a scheduled chat shows how it repeats, its next and last run, its prompt and a Stop button. The tray menu shows the next runs as well.

list.name: MCP Server Configuration
list.about: Users can add their own MCP servers so agents get extra tools. In the settings view they list, edit and rename servers as text, or search the official MCP Registry and add a server it lists. The editor text is parsed into server definitions and saved in the store. When a session starts, the definitions are converted to ACP form and passed to the agent together with the Workbench's own browser server.

list.name: CodeGraph Index
list.about: A project can have a CodeGraph index of its symbols that agents query. The main process reads the project's index, syncs it and caches the result, then reports when it changes. A parent folder's index doesn't count as the project's own. The orientation card shows whether the project is indexed and has a button to start indexing, and the status bar shows the index state.

list.name: Knowledge Vault
list.about: Each project can have a knowledge vault of Markdown notes describing its modules and concepts. The main process maintains and rebuilds the vault. It outlines files, signs modules so it can tell which have changed, and sends batched briefs to an agent to write the summaries. Wiki-links in notes resolve to note links when shown in chat Markdown. The graph pane draws the vault as a rotating graph, with nodes sized by link count and colored by project area.

list.name: Project Intake
list.about: When a project is new to the Workbench, an intake questionnaire is scheduled for it. The main process first scans the folder for its stack, dependencies and notable source findings. From that scan it generates intake questions, using fallback questions if generation fails. The user's answers become session rules that later chats in the project follow.

list.name: Agent Questions
list.about: An agent can stop in the middle of a turn to ask the user a question. The main process parses the question out of the agent's output and sends a prompt event to the renderer. The chat shows the question and its options. When the user answers or the question is dropped, a settle event closes it and the turn continues.

list.name: Activity Feed
list.about: The activity feed is a separate window showing what every chat's agent is doing. The main process tracks running turns, notices and permission activity for each chat. The feed groups tool events into turns per chat, with timings. Selecting a file edit opens a side-by-side code diff computed line by line.

list.name: Background Attention
list.about: The Workbench keeps running when its window is closed, and it tells the user when a chat needs them. The main process handles the window lifecycle, keeps a single instance and hides the app to the menu bar tray. When a chat finishes while the app is unfocused, the dock badge updates and a system notification appears. The tray menu lists bots, their next runs and chats that are waiting.

list.name: Chat Media and Visuals
list.about: Chats can show images, videos, YouTube transcripts and HTML visuals that agents draw. A custom protocol serves media files to the chat, and media paths are resolved only within allowed root folders. An agent-drawn HTML visual is stored and shown in a sandboxed frame. The Markdown renderer recognizes image and video sources and visual blocks and draws them inline. YouTube links are parsed to a video id and the video's captions are fetched as a transcript.

list.name: Slash Commands
list.about: Typing a slash in the composer opens a list of commands. Each agent has its own command definitions, and the list is filtered as the user types. On send, the input is parsed as a command and handled either by the Workbench or by the agent session.

list.name: Themes
list.about: The UI's colors and fonts come from a theme file. Three built-in themes ship with the app, and users can save, import, export and delete their own. Activating a theme applies its colors to the document and adds the font stylesheet links it needs. A React provider holds the current theme and exposes it through `useTheme`. The theme editor changes colors with pickers and shows them on a live preview.

list.name: Voice
list.about: Voice input and output run locally in web workers, using onnxruntime-web. Whisper turns dictated speech into text, one request at a time, with a UI-thread fallback. Supertonic turns text into audio. Before a reply is read aloud, its Markdown is turned into speakable text, the language is chosen, and echoes of the user's own request are dropped. A provider tracks listening, transcribing and speaking and exposes them through `useVoice`. The settings modal sets the voice language and speed, and the main process handles the voice model status and microphone permission.

list.name: Progress Cues
list.about: While a long turn runs, the Workbench gives short progress updates so the user knows what the agent is doing. The renderer tracks each chat's running activity and decides when a progress update should be spoken. For a running shell task, the main process finds the latest output line to report. The speech queue lets these status lines jump ahead of reply sentences that are waiting to be read.

list.name: Pull Request Watching
list.about: A chat can be linked to a GitHub pull request. The main process links the PR to the chat, then watches it and reports status changes. The chat pane shows a PR bar with the current status.
